title: When one customer starts choosing your market

Product Strategy Business Strategy Software Development Enterpreneurship When one customer starts choosing your market Salman Asif 3 min read · Oct 28, 2026 -- Listen Share A profitable contract can restrict the next sale. Evaluate the commitments, not just the funded work. A large contract can make it harder to sell to the next customer. Customer-funded development can be a good opportunity. The problem has a buyer, the work has a budget, and the business can learn through a real commitment rather than a speculative roadmap. But the contract can shape more than what gets built. Its commitments can also shape who the company can still serve. A delivery promise can become a market constraint Consider a fictional software company negotiating with a national distributor. The distributor will fund development around its classifications and approval rules. Suppose the company also agrees not to change the shared approval workflow during the distributor’s six-month peak season. This is an explicit restriction in our hypothetical, not something inferred from funding or an ordinary release calendar. Another intended buyer needs a different approval sequence introduced during that period before it can use the product. The engineering team might be capable of making that change. There may be credible demand for it. Neither resolves the conflict with the first commitment. The company would need to reconcile those promises before offering the second buyer a timetable it can honor. A technically achievable sale may not be commercially available on the terms that buyer needs. That is a different question from whether shared development is economical. Even useful, reusable software can sit behind commitments that limit the market it can serve. Choose the limit consciously A specialist business serving a small number of demanding customers is not automatically inferior to a broadly repeatable software product. A substantial account can justify an engagement whose value stands on its own. An anchor customer can also fund a capability that other buyers genuinely need. The mistake is not accepting customer-specific work. It is treating the wider product strategy as unchanged when the accompanying promises restrict it. In this hypothetical, leadership has several possible directions. It could accept that buyers needing a change during the restricted period are outside the offer. That may be sensible if the account is valuable enough and the narrower market fits the strategy. It could negotiate a more bounded restriction, protecting the distributor’s deployed workflow without freezing the shared offer. That requires agreement; it is not a freedom the supplier can simply assume. Or it could investigate separating the account-specific workflow from the shared product. That might preserve more flexibility, but it creates another investment decision rather than removing the problem for free. Flexibility has obligations too Separate versions may require additional testing, support, and maintenance. Changes intended for one customer may still affect shared components. The original commitment may need to be renegotiated even if technical separation is possible. Those are possibilities to investigate, not a prescribed architecture or a claim that separation always works. The comparison should therefore include both sides: the value of the contract and the obligations required to retain the future offer leadership wants to make. A smaller restriction may be enough. Separation may be worthwhile. A deliberate specialist engagement may be the better business. Before accepting the deal, bring the proposed promise into the product and commercial decision together. Identify the future requirements it would prevent the business from serving, whether the boundary can be narrowed, and what retaining flexibility would cost. This is not a reason to promise every buyer a different product. It is a reason to know which buyers a valuable promise will exclude before treating the contract as uncomplicated progress. The question isn’t only whether the contract pays for the work. It’s which future customers the business remains free to serve after making that promise.
